newsitem.title: USA: Senate passes $21.1 billion energy bill.
newsitem.headline: Senate passes $21.1 billion energy bill.

text.p: The Senate Wednesday voted 99-0 for a $21.1 billion spending bill for various energy and water programs, with about half of the money for nuclear weapons and cleanup programs.

The Clinton administration wanted $23 billion for the spending bill for programs next year, and said it objected that the Senate provided just $343 million of the $1 billion it sought to pay for new contracts with private companies that are decontaminating and cleaning former nuclear weapons production sites.
The White House said failure to allow more privatizing of the complex and dangerous work would raise costs and jeopardize legally binding deadlines for cleanups.
But Republicans said they were not certain the Energy Department was capable of managing the technically challenging and expensive new contracts.
The Senate shifted $283 million of those funds to nuclear stockpile stewardship and management programs, which the White House said it did not want.

The bill also would provide $664.7 million for non-defense nuclear waste and clean-up programs, including $350 million for programs to manage waste from nuclear power plants and other non-defense sources.
The White House said the bill was $30 million below the White House request for work to see if Yucca Mountain in Nevada will be a suitable dump site for waste from nuclear reactors and other sources.
The bill also would spend $16.4 billion to run the Energy Department, $633 million above last year, but $2 billion below the White House request.
It also would provide $967 million for energy research, $102 million above this year but $117 million below the administration's request.
It would spend $2.2 billion on science programs such as high energy physics, nuclear physics, and biological and environmental research.

The Senate rejected an amendment to halt spending on the controversial Animas-La Plata water project in southern Colorado, and kept $6 million in the bill that the administration wanted to fund negotiations to revise the project.
